ads.headline: Carbon transmitter capsules
ads.body: Sealed capsule and contact set, from the electrical drawers. An older pattern than the telephone company carries, which is why we still have one. Ask at the counter.
ads.source: game/data/shop_inventory.json carbon_transmitter_capsule
ads.art: A tiny man on a ladder before a towering wall of little drawers, holding up one small round capsule like a pearl.

ads.headline: Rubber protectant, service bottle
ads.body: Twenty-five cents, stopper included. Dresses the rubber washers in your fire-hose fittings. It does not replace a missing washer, certify the line or put out the fire. We have been asked.
ads.source: game/data/orison_v2/fire_maintenance_stock.json fire_hose_rubber_protectant
ads.art: A pompous man in a fire helmet dabs a little brush at a hose coupling, while flames rise calmly out of the window behind him.

ads.headline: Fire-hose coupling gaskets, ten cents
ads.body: A rubber washer of the fire-cabinet union's retained pattern, in a small pressed tin. It is the cheapest thing in the cabinet, and the only one that stops the water going sideways.
ads.source: game/data/orison_v2/fire_maintenance_stock.json fire_hose_spare_gasket
ads.art: A fireman stands soaked by water spraying sideways from a hose joint, while a single small washer lies on the ground at his feet.

ads.headline: Soap flakes, scouring powder, matches
ads.body: Flakes twelve cents, twenty washes. Scouring powder ten cents. Kitchen matches five cents the box of fifty. Paint and sash cord also, if the matches go badly.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json soap_flakes, scouring_powder, matches
ads.art: A man strikes one match in a kitchen and his eyebrows are gone, a neat black oval around his startled eyes.

ads.headline: Silk flex for the man with a position
ads.body: Woven silk at a good price by the yard, rubber for the rest of you. Your visitors will not look at your furniture. They will look at your flex.
ads.source: Bible VIII.4 cloth-braided cable; newspaper 1928-11-15 record: Valves 6 for 96 cents, up 2
ads.art: A man in a patched coat and no shoes proudly holds up a magnificent plaited cord to a visitor, with bare boards and a crate behind him.

ads.headline: Valves by the six-sleeve
ads.body: Newark receiving valves in the printed sleeve, about a dollar the six. Keep a spare in the drawer and not in the window, where the glass tells the street.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-11-15 record: Valves 6 for 96 cents, up 2; Bible VIII.4 valves are a consumable
ads.art: A man on a stoop hides six long glass bulbs under his coat, their tips poking out like a row of teeth, with burglars' eyes in the dark behind him.

ads.headline: One spare, with permission
ads.body: Bring the resident's permission and we cut one spare. The original stays with the resident. Blanks in brass and nickel on the board. Padlocks on the rail.
ads.source: game/scripts/game/door_keyring.gd copy_prompt, make_copy; game/data/orison_v2/locksmith_fittings.json
ads.art: A big man with a bowler holds a very large key while a tiny locksmith at a cutting wheel points sternly up at a blank paper slip in the man's other hand.

ads.headline: We have your key somewhere
ads.body: Hundreds of blanks on brass hooks, sorted by profile. Every one opens something. The locksmith would rather not say what, and he will want that permission in writing.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 3, the key board; game/scripts/game/door_keyring.gd
ads.art: A man stands on tiptoe at a wall of hundreds of hanging keys, with a single loose key falling and landing on his head.

ads.headline: The Borough Record, two cents
ads.body: Queens County's paper of record, every morning, from the rack in the Arcade and the coin boxes on the kerb. Numbers, names and committee titles, in the order they occurred.
ads.source: design/ORISON_NEWSPAPERS_2026-10-23.md section 1
ads.art: A stiff gentleman reads a broadsheet held perfectly square while a horse eats the far corner of it.

ads.headline: The Loud Speaker, one cent
ads.body: If it happened, we heard it. Half the price of the other paper and three times the sale. Read it before your employer does, and keep it from your mother.
ads.source: design/ORISON_NEWSPAPERS_2026-10-23.md section 1
ads.art: A paper boy shouts so hard his cap flies off and a row of pigeons is blown backward off a ledge.

ads.headline: Quell tonic, five cents the bottle
ads.body: Cold from the case at the News & Cigars counter. It quells. Our lawyer would like us to stop there, and so we shall.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json quell_tonic (the brand name predates this ad; no resident meant)
ads.art: A very red-faced shouting man with steam at his ears takes one swig of a small bottle and becomes a perfectly still, smiling statue.

ads.headline: A bar of chocolate, five cents
ads.body: The same size as last year, the man says. So are you, he says. Take it home, or eat it in the Arcade where nobody counts.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json chocolate
ads.art: A large man hides behind a very narrow lamppost in the rain, eating a chocolate bar with his back to the viewer.

ads.headline: Milk, eggs, bread and valves
ads.body: Meridian milk, fifteen cents. Eggs, forty-five the dozen. White loaf, nine cents. Valves beside the cigarettes, in the sleeve. All from the one counter, before the first trolley.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json milk, eggs, white_bread; Bible VIII.4 valves sold at the bodega
ads.art: A grocer weighs an egg in one pan of a scale against a glowing radio valve in the other, with the scale exactly level.

ads.headline: Rat-trap cheddar
ads.body: Thirty-two cents the pound. Named for its use and its reputation. The rats of Queens have been known to write in. So far we have only their word.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json cheddar
ads.art: A rat in a small necktie sits at a dinner table with a napkin, carving a wedge of cheese out of a sprung trap.

ads.headline: Harukiya shoyu, twenty cents
ads.body: Sold at the bodega, twenty tablespoons to the bottle. We can tell you about the sauce. We cannot tell you anything about the rest of the Harukiya, and neither can they.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json shoyu
ads.art: A shopkeeper holds up one small bottle while holding a finger to his lips, and a closed door with a single lit lantern sits behind him.

ads.headline: Peerless lager, twelve cents
ads.body: A lawful cereal beverage, and it has been described to the sergeant as such. The sergeant has had two and agrees. Peerless is sold by the bottle, without remark.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json lager (the canon stock name; the 'lawful' claim is the joke)
ads.art: A policeman leans on a shop counter at a precarious angle holding up a bottle, his helmet slid down over one eye.

ads.headline: Fall River smoked sausage
ads.body: Thirty cents the twelve ounces. It keeps. Holloway's prepared mustard goes with it, twelve cents, and Astoria cream if you are expecting someone you wish to impress.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json smoked_sausage, mustard, cream
ads.art: A dog on a street corner tows a long string of sausages away behind him, with a butcher far behind holding the other end.

ads.headline: Yesterday's rolls, today
ads.body: Six for a nickel. They were fresh when you could not afford them. Gingersnaps a dime the dozen, dripping eight cents, and spent coffee grounds free to anyone who asks.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json day_old_rolls, gingersnaps, beef_dripping, spent_coffee
ads.art: A customer knocks a roll against the counter and it dents the counter, while the counterman calmly goes on wiping a cup.

ads.headline: Coffee, pie and two receiving cabinets
ads.body: Sandwiches at the counter. Hot coffee from the twin urns. Pickled eggs in the jar. Two cabinets in the corner, which nobody has remarked on, and neither shall we.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 5, the flair
ads.art: A man eats pie at a plain wooden counter, ignoring a huge gleaming machine with dials, sparks and tall antennae right behind his stool.

ads.headline: Our carbonator has never been wrong
ads.body: Soda from the marble fountain, nickel taps, a row of syrups. The milk shake is mixed on green enamel. The customer has been wrong a number of times.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 5, soda fountain
ads.art: A soda jerk pulls the tap and a gush of foam lifts a stout man and his stool clean off the floor.

ads.headline: Soda at the druggist's
ads.body: Four stools at the marble fountain, halfway down the shop. It is the only thing we sell of which we can say with confidence what it will do.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 11; design/ORISON_KITCHENS_2026-10-24.md
ads.art: A man on a stool sips soda through a straw, surrounded on every side by rows of gloomy medicine bottles with skulls on them.

ads.headline: Spices and bicarbonate of soda
ads.body: Cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, bay, paprika, mustard powder, from the drawers. Bicarbonate five cents. Nobody has ever been cured of anything by our bay leaves, but the stew improved.
ads.source: game/data/kitchen/groceries.json cinnamon, bay_leaves, baking_soda
ads.art: A patient in a bed has a large bay leaf laid on his forehead by a solemn druggist, with a pot of stew steaming beside him.

ads.headline: For cuts, carbolic and a clean rag
ads.body: Boil the rag. Keep the cut dry. If it reddens, send for us early. The show globes in our window are coloured water and are not for sale.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 11; Bible VIII.1, the septic cut
ads.art: A man with one tiny bandaged finger sits up in bed dictating solemnly into a big gleaming horn, while a doctor beside him shrugs.

ads.headline: A photograph is an occasion
ads.body: Plates, paper and chemicals by the box. Everyone in Queens has a record of your voice. Nobody has a picture of your face. Come in while you have one.
ads.source: Bible VIII.4 recording is cheap, photography is dear; game/data/orison_v2/photo_stock.json
ads.art: A family stands rigid in a row in Sunday clothes, with a horse at the end, all holding their breath before a camera on a tripod.

ads.headline: Sets repaired on the premises
ads.body: Your set on our cradle, its back off and its valves standing. Scope and signal generator on the bench. The schematic is pasted in your lid, and we can read it.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 4; game/data/orison_v2/radio_stock.json; Bible VIII.4 everything is repairable
ads.art: A repairman in a patched apron peers into a dazzling machine full of glowing tubes and lightning, by the light of one small candle.

ads.headline: Unredeemed articles for sale
ads.body: A violin, a sewing machine, a camera, surgical instruments, a mantel clock, a wedding ring in a small envelope. Each held its full term. Each with a number.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 7, the unredeemed shelf
ads.art: A tall dark wall of shelves with tagged objects, and one small man looking up at it, holding only his hat.

ads.headline: A used valve has seen things
ads.body: Second-hand valves on Jackson Avenue, at whatever they were this morning. They have one more evening in them, probably. Your overcoat is still here, and it asks after you.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-12-30 speaker: Second-hand valves hit thirty-five cents
ads.art: A shivering man in shirtsleeves in the snow carries home a single glass valve, cradled in both hands like a kitten.

ads.headline: Gas mantles: we have none
ads.body: We have no more of the old pattern, and neither has the company. A workroom that has spent its dozen should write to its management office, and then make them last.
ads.source: game/data/mail_catalog.json pkg_gas_mantles; game/scripts/props/orison_v2_mantle_carton.gd
ads.art: A shopkeeper turns out empty pockets before his wall of drawers while a customer holds up a lamp whose mantle has crumbled into a little heap.

ads.headline: Hear what the pipes are saying
ads.body: One contact microphone, hard-wired, with alligator clip and a hand-wound coil of shielded cable. By post only. They will say it whether you listen or not, so you may as well.
ads.source: game/data/mail_catalog.json pkg_contact_mic
ads.art: A man in a nightshirt lies on a cellar floor with a clip on a pipe and headphones on, as a huge rat beside him listens to the other earpiece.

ads.headline: Your shirts are still here
ads.body: Brown paper, string and a ticket. Some of these have waited since the war. We have kept them clean, which is more than can be said of the gentleman who left them.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 1, the ticket rail and parcel wall
ads.art: A laundryman on a tall ladder at a wall of parcels hands down a package to a very old man with a beard to his knees, holding a ticket.

ads.headline: You can smell our work from here
ads.body: Heels and soles on the finishing machine: brushes, drums, wheels and a belt. Loud, filthy, and the reason the street smells like this. Your shoes will come back improved.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 2, the finishing machine
ads.art: A cobbler holds a boot to a roaring belt machine as a dust cloud rolls down the street and the pedestrians hold their noses.

ads.headline: Sixteen chairs, and no hurry
ads.body: Front room with palms and folding chairs. Charges explained beforehand, in writing. Your voice on a good clear record costs little. A photograph is extra.
ads.source: design/SHOP_INTERIOR_BUILD_GUIDE.md section 8; Bible VIII.4
ads.art: Four rows of empty folding chairs facing a low empty bier, and one undertaker alone in the front row, patiently checking his watch.

ads.headline: Dictate it. It types itself.
ads.body: Speak your letter to the cabinet, and it comes out in clean type with the spelling better than yours. Second-hand from eleven dollars. Your chilblains are your own affair.
ads.source: Bible VIII.2: dictates a letter to a machine that transcribes it
ads.art: A man in bed in hat and scarf, an icicle on his nose, dictates to a sleek shining machine that spits out a long sheet of paper over the frozen floor.

ads.headline: It answers when you are out
ads.body: Our answering cabinet takes the message and is civil to your creditors. It is often more civil than you. Your wife has asked if it can stay and you can go.
ads.source: Bible VIII.2 Rule of Signal (a signal stored and reproduced)
ads.art: A husband with a suitcase stands on the stoop in the rain, while indoors a woman has her feet up beside a large cabinet with a horn, both content.

ads.headline: Ice at the door, by the hundredweight
ads.body: The block on your icebox, the tray beneath it, and the same horse as before. Our machines have not improved in any way. Neither has the weather.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-05-01 record: Light rate of 7.5 cents and ice at 45 cents; Bible VIII.4 ice and coal
ads.art: An ice man with tongs and a big block trudges past a radio tower, a horse beside him looking equally unimpressed.

ads.headline: Long-life receiving valves
ads.body: The same glass that lights the borough, with a longer life and a longer price. Ask your Arcade hardware counter. Sold in the sleeve; six hundred hands; two shifts.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-05-22 record: Valves at a dollar the six; newspaper 1929-01-02 speaker: Newark lights up the valve works
ads.art: A long line of tiny workers in caps carry one giant glowing valve on their shoulders like a coffin, out of a factory gate.

ads.headline: The answering doll, three dollars fifty
ads.body: She says six words. The maker has examined her at Newark and finds nothing to correct. Should she say otherwise at your house, the proprietress asks you to bring her back.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-12-13 record: Arcade toy counter sells out of answering dolls; newspaper 1929-01-05 speaker: Newark says the chatty dolls were perfectly quiet at home
ads.art: A big stern father in a nightcap creeps out of a child's room backward, candle high, with a small doll sitting up in the dark bed behind him.

ads.headline: Listening Act door notices, in brass
ads.body: The Act wants a notice posted at your door. Ours is screwed on properly, by a man who does this. Licence is your own business at five dollars a year.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-11-14 record: Listening Act drafted in Albany; newspaper 1929-07-01 record: Listening Act licences required from today
ads.art: A workman screws a big blank brass plate over the entire front door of a tiny house, with the owner trapped looking out of the keyhole.

ads.headline: The room consent book
ads.body: Fifty pages. Every party to the room signs before anyone says anything further. Husbands find it clears the air. Dogs may mark with a paw.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-03-28 record: Senate committee adopts the bedroom, insurance and confession amendments
ads.art: A man in a nightshirt holds out a clipboard and pen at the bedside, while his wife reads on and the cat is already signing.

ads.headline: Your pipes will testify
ads.body: Our licensed adjuster listens to the burst and tells you when, where and whose fault. He will not mend it. Policies by the room. Ticketed under the Act.
ads.source: Bible VIII.1 acoustic telegraphy for insurance work; newspaper 1929-03-28 record: Senate committee adopts the bedroom, insurance and confession amendments
ads.art: An adjuster in a bowler kneels up to his chest in flood water, holding a stethoscope against a spouting pipe and taking notes.

ads.headline: Your parlour will back you up
ads.body: A record of everything said in the room, admissible in court. Your side of the argument, preserved. So is hers. We recommend you consider that before you buy.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-02-28 speaker: Lasko jury asks for a replay
ads.art: A man stands triumphantly pointing at a horn machine in the parlour while it blasts a huge jagged shout that knocks his own hat off.

ads.headline: The listening chair
ads.body: Upholstered ear wings, a shelf for the set, and a spring that has been sat on by two previous gentlemen. You can hear everything. It will hurt only where you sit.
ads.source: Bible VIII.2 (signal advanced, the rest 1927 and second-hand); Bible VIII.4 'The kitchen is 1890. The parlour is 1970'
ads.art: A man sinks into a vast winged armchair with his ears cupped by its wings, a broken spring bursting out under him through the seat.

ads.headline: Party-line manners, ten cents
ads.body: When to speak. When to stop breathing. What to do when you recognize the second voice. Forty pages, revised for the present state of the wires, and approved by no one.
ads.source: Bible VIII.4 dial-less telephones; newspaper 1929-01-24 speaker: Three minutes, please
ads.art: Six identical men on six stools in a row all listen on one long shared receiver, their heads tilted the same way, one with a finger up for silence.

ads.headline: Now truly portable
ads.body: Our new portable wet cell needs only two men and a hand truck. Go anywhere your friends will still have you. Acid sold separately. Trousers also sold separately.
ads.source: Bible VIII.4 batteries are enormous
ads.art: Two men strain to push a huge crate on a hand truck up a hill, with a tiny radio on top, while a picnicker waits in a field far away.

ads.headline: Parts for Vantry sets
ads.body: The makers have been gone for years. Parts are not made. We have one screw, and it is on somebody's lien notice. Repairs by reading the lid, and prayer.
ads.source: Bible VIII.3 Vantry & Co. no longer exists; newspaper 1929-03-10 record: All twelve screws on the Arcade's lien notices
ads.art: A repairman with a pair of tweezers and a magnifying glass holds up one tiny screw, under a colossal silent machine with cobwebs.

ads.headline: Vantry service sets, second-hand
ads.body: Works perfectly. Older than the tenant. Nobody knows what half of it does, and it does that perfectly as well. No repairs by the maker. No maker.
ads.source: Bible VIII.3; Bible VIII.5 service set
ads.art: A proud pawnbroker pats a huge machine with a lightning bolt coming from it, while a thin customer holds his hat on with both hands.

ads.headline: Record one ordinary Sunday
ads.body: Members seal their records in copper for the people of 1978. Dues modest. Meetings monthly in Jamaica. The committee welcomes guests, who may sit at the back.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-11-18 record: Phonautograph Society asks the borough to record 'one ordinary Sunday'
ads.art: A family at dinner chews politely as a large man in a frock coat holds a recording horn over the roast, and the dog howls into it.

ads.headline: Phonautograph blanks by the dozen
ads.body: Clean wax, in the sleeve, for records of Queens. We do not ask what you will put on them. Unwise members have ended up in a cupboard, voted down by two.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-01-05 record: Phonautograph Society divides 19 to 17; game/data/newspapers (No. 23)
ads.art: A committee of whiskered men hold a tall cupboard door shut with all their weight, while a single wax cylinder sits behind it, unbothered.

ads.headline: Bury it for 1978
ads.body: Copper case, soldered lid, room for thirteen mothers or one Mr. Abbot. Your descendants may hear you. They will have nothing else to do, and they will be sorry.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-06-16 record: Grieve capsule sealed beneath the Flushing library's reading room floor; Phonautograph Society
ads.art: A bewhiskered man in a frock coat, still talking, is lowered into a hole in a big copper box, with a calm woman holding the lid.

ads.headline: Records with the tone removed
ads.body: Meeting fortnightly at the Flushing Free Library. Where possible. Mr. Moss, pharmacist, presides. We do not say what the tone is. We have only taken it out, where possible.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-07-10 record: Phonautograph Circle of Flushing meets; newspaper 1929-07-15 record: Phonautograph Circle to meet fortnightly
ads.art: A pharmacist in a white coat holds up a pair of tongs with a curly black squiggle in them, drawn out of a record, and looks for where to put it.

ads.headline: Felt for under your bedposts
ads.body: Four pads, twenty-five cents. Does not quiet the Hum, which the company states isn't any concern of ours or yours. It only stops the bed from joining in.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-11-13 record: Astoria petition on the Hum; newspaper 1929-08-06 speaker: Rastin's meter says the Hum
ads.art: A man in bed clings to the mattress as the whole bed walks across the room on its shaking legs, with one felt pad left behind on the floor.

ads.headline: Tune your flat to forty-one
ads.body: Strike the bar. Now it is your idea. No claim is made for this device regarding sleep, marriage, the light company or the source of any tone, which remains unknown.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-01-29 record: Dr. Rastin's readings find 41 cycles at all 23 places
ads.art: A man in a nightshirt stands on a chair and strikes a big tuning fork with a spoon, and every picture on the wall tilts the same way.

ads.headline: Bring earplugs or a petition
ads.body: Wax earplugs ten cents the pair. Our petition counter is your own affair. Keeps out everything but the thing you were trying to keep out.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-12-31 speaker: Hum petition signs up 2,140 voices
ads.art: A man with enormous wax plugs in his ears smiles in a blissful calm while a brass band marches over him.

ads.headline: The home cycle meter
ads.body: For the householder who wishes to read the figure for himself. It will read forty-one. The makers do not say why, and the company states it does not concern the company.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-01-29 record: Dr. Rastin's readings find 41 cycles; newspaper 1929-08-13 record: Night tone two fifths stronger
ads.art: A pompous man on a roof at night holds up a big dial meter, with the needle bent right round and pointing at his own head.

ads.headline: Our load is unchanged
ads.body: Domestic current at the published rate. Your bill shows a credit, which the company does not call a refund. All other questions do not concern the company.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-11-13 record: Astoria petition on the Hum; newspaper 1929-07-01 record: Light company's July bills
ads.art: A tiny man in a top hat stands on a huge bare lightbulb with his arms folded, as a little crowd below waves paper slips at him.

ads.headline: Three minutes, please
ads.body: Lift the receiver and an operator answers. Your party is available when the operator says so. Please do not address the animal at Position 43, or send her anything.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-01-24 speaker: Three minutes, please; newspaper 1928-12-08 speaker: Cat takes over the Queens switchboard
ads.art: A cat lies asleep along a long switchboard, one paw on a plug, with a sergeant standing behind her holding his hat in his hands.

ads.headline: The sardine with a following
ads.body: Packed in oil, sold by the tin, and posted to no address in particular. Some of our customers do not give their names. We never ask. Neither does the cat.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-03-07 speaker: Sergeant calls at the Exchange, and Party Line won't put him through
ads.art: A cat wearing a false moustache buys a tin of fish at a post-office window, while the clerk looks the other way.

ads.headline: Map pins by the gross
ads.body: For the gentleman following a certain station about the Sound. We sell the pins. We sell the string. The lines still won't meet. We do not sell an explanation.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-02-24 speaker: Where's WORS? Pike takes three bearings; newspaper 1929-06-23 speaker: Where's WORS? Pin ninety-eight
ads.art: A Radio Division man in a launch, surrounded by water, holds a huge pin over a map on his lap, as the map is entirely full of pins.

ads.headline: We make no claim as to 1610
ads.body: Our sets receive all licensed stations on the dial. Should yours receive any other, the maker asks you to write to the Radio Division and not to us.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-11-14 record: Hunters Point tug reports transmitter on the river at 1610
ads.art: A salesman with a broad grin holds a radio set at arm's length with tongs, his face turned away and his eyes shut.

ads.headline: For the licence queue
ads.body: Corn plasters, ten cents. Bring your form. If you have no form you will be sent to the back and given one. Bring two plasters.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-04-25 speaker: Licence queue forms at seven
ads.art: A very long line of men wind out of a government door and around the block, with one small man at the front, grown a white beard, handed a form.

ads.headline: Rent is due at the box
ads.body: Rent payable at the post box. Enquiries are not answered. Notices are fixed with good screws. The company has no further statement, and no office in which to make it.
ads.source: newspaper 1928-12-05 record: Borough Hall writes a third time to Signal Ground Rents Inc.; newspaper 1929-03-10 record: All twelve screws
ads.art: A very small post box on a very tall pole in an empty field, with a crowd of tenants holding money up on tiptoe.

ads.headline: Postal cards by the hundred
ads.body: One-cent stamp, one card, and you have thought of another. Your family has asked us to stop selling them to you. We have told them we are very sorry.
ads.source: newspaper 1929-06-02 speaker: The Pun Derby opens tomorrow
ads.art: A mailman staggers under a heaving sack toward a smiling man at a little desk, who already holds up one more card, as a horse looks on, depressed.

ads.headline: Learn to read a schematic
ads.body: Every set made has its drawing pasted in the lid. Twenty lessons by post, and you are a repairman. There is still no cure for your cough, but you can record it clearly.
ads.source: Bible VIII.4 everything is repairable; Bible VIII.1 there is still no penicillin
ads.art: A man coughs into a horn in bed, with a thermometer in his mouth and a set's open lid on his lap, soldering it happily.

ads.headline: Have it said properly
ads.body: Ten minutes on good wax for a dollar. For wills, apologies and the location of certain papers. We attend at home. Bring your own doctor, if you still have one.
ads.source: Bible VIII.1: a building wired well enough to record her saying so
ads.art: An old man sits up in bed with a horn at his mouth, lecturing loudly, while a line of relatives wait with handkerchiefs and an undertaker checks his watch.

ads.headline: The inside-window scraper
ads.body: Nickel a piece. Takes the frost off your glass from the inside, as nature did not intend. Leaves you a clear view of the aerial you paid for.
ads.source: Bible VIII.2: a tenant scrapes ice off the inside of her window
ads.art: A man in an overcoat indoors scrapes a frosted window with a little blade, and through the clear patch a huge shining radio mast stands outside.
